claim: Drosophila Perlecan is encoded by the gene terribly reduced optic lobes (trol).
source: The Drosophila Perlecan homolog is encoded by the gene terribly reduced optic lobes (trol) (Datta and Kankel, 1992; Friedrich et al., 2000; Voigt et al., 2002)
evidence: The statement is directly supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The trol locus resides on the X chromosome and encodes 25 predicted Perlecan splice variants ranging in size from 2853 to 4489 amino acids.
source: Drosophila Perlecan is encoded by the trol locus, which resides on the X chromosome and encodes 25 predicted Perlecan splice variants ranging in size from 2853 to 4489 amino acids (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim references Figure 1A which shows the trol locus structure, and provides specific numerical data about splice variants and amino acid sizes.

claim: Drosophila Perlecan clustered in a phylogenetic tree with other Perlecan homologs and distinct from the Agrin family.
source: Drosophila Perlecan clustered in a leaf with other Perlecan homologs and distinct from the Agrin family.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis described in the methods and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Drosophila contains glutamatergic NMJs and lacks an Agrin homolog.
source: Drosophila contains glutamatergic NMJs and lacks an Agrin homolog (Littleton and Ganetzky, 2000).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: TrolGFP was enriched along nerve bundles and present at lower levels on the surface of body wall muscles.
source: TrolGFP was enriched along nerve bundles (Figure 1C–F) and present at lower levels on the surface of body wall muscles (Figure 1C and G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1C-I.

claim: Perlecan has been previously observed within the neural lamella surrounding the VNC and peripheral nerves.
source: Indeed, Perlecan has been previously observed within the neural lamella surrounding the VNC and peripheral nerves (Brink et al., 2012; Skeath et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TrolGFP did not display synaptic enrichment beyond the homogenous expression over the entire muscle surface.
source: Although immunogold electron microscopy (EM) identified Perlecan in the subsynaptic reticulum (SSR) surrounding NMJs (Kamimura et al., 2013), TrolGFP did not display synaptic enrichment beyond the homogenous expression over the entire muscle surface (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 1G-I and contrasts with previous EM findings cited.

claim: TrolGFP was eliminated by co-expression of trol RNAi, with no signal observed along nerve bundles or on the muscle surface.
source: TrolGFP was eliminated by co-expression of the RNAi, with no signal observed along nerve bundles or on the muscle surface (Figure 1D–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing loss of TrolGFP signal upon RNAi knockdown.

claim: The TrolGFP line displayed normal NMJ growth and maintenance.
source: The TrolGFP line also displayed normal NMJ growth and maintenance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in contrast to trol mutants (see below)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of bouton numbers shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Male trolnull larvae are smaller than their heterozygous female trolnull/+ counterparts and display disrupted locomotion and lethality during the 3rd instar stage.
source: Male trolnull larvae are smaller than their heterozygous female trolnull/+counterparts and display disrupted locomotion and lethality during the 3rd instar stage (Datta and Kankel, 1992; Voigt et al., 2002).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many trol NMJs displayed Dlg+ boutons that lacked presynaptic Cpx.
source: Although some trolnull/y larvae had intact NMJs, many trol NMJs displayed Dlg +boutons that lacked presynaptic Cpx (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The presence of postsynaptic 'footprints' lacking presynaptic material is a defining feature of mutants that undergo synaptic retraction.
source: The presence of postsynaptic 'footprints' lacking presynaptic material is a defining feature of mutants that undergo synaptic retraction (Eaton et al., 2002; Graf et al., 2011; Koch et al., 2008; Pielage et al., 2008; Pielage et al., 2005).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Trolnull mutants displayed fewer synaptic boutons compared to control NMJs in abdominal segments A3-A5.
source: Trolnull mutants also displayed fewer synaptic boutons (Figure 2B), in addition to increased synaptic footprints (Figure 2C), compared to control NMJs in abdominal segments A3-A5 (bouton number p values: 0.0379 for A3, 0.0012 for A4,<0.0001 for A5).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance values provided.

claim: The trolnull phenotype was more severe in posterior abdominal segments.
source: Consistent with other retraction mutants (Graf et al., 2011), the trolnull phenotype was more severe in posterior abdominal segments (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data in Figure 2B and C showing increasing severity in posterior segments, and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: NMJs showing severe synaptic retraction were only observed in trolnull larvae, with increasing severity in posterior abdominal segments.
source: NMJs showing severe synaptic retraction, defined by retraction footprints and decreased number of synaptic boutons two standard deviations compared to controls, were only observed in trolnull larvae, with increasing severity in posterior abdominal segments (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Df(1)ED411/trolnull NMJs had significantly reduced bouton number, with 50% of NMJs showing postsynaptic footprints.
source: In contrast, Df(1)ED411/trolnull NMJs had significantly reduced bouton number (p=0.0048), with 50% of NMJs showing postsynaptic footprints (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C with statistical significance provided.

claim: Expression of UAS-trol-RNAi.2 with the ubiquitous tubulin-Gal4 driver resulted in reduced bouton number, with >65% of NMJs showing postsynaptic footprints.
source: In addition, expression of UAS-trol-RNAi.2 with the ubiquitous tubulin-Gal4 driver resulted in reduced bouton number, with >65% of NMJs showing postsynaptic footprints compared to RNAi or Gal4 only controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Trolnull Is NMJs displayed a significant reduction in bouton number compared to heterozygous controls.
source: Similar to Ib, trolnull Is NMJs displayed a significant reduction in bouton number (p=0.0011 A3, p=0.0238 A4, p=0.0068 A5), with >30% showing severe retraction phenotypes compared to heterozygous controls (trolnull/+, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C with statistical significance values provided.

claim: Synaptic retraction occurs across all MN subtypes in 3rd instar larvae lacking Perlecan.
source: Together, these data indicate synaptic retraction occurs across all MN subtypes in 3rd instar larvae lacking Perlecan.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of retraction in Ib, Is, and type II/III MNs.

claim: A previous study identified changes in pre- and postsynaptic Wg levels at trol mutant NMJs, suggesting Perlecan restricts Wg diffusion within the synaptic cleft.
source: A previous study identified changes in pre- and postsynaptic Wg levels at trol mutant NMJs, suggesting Perlecan restricts Wg diffusion within the synaptic cleft. The absence of Perlecan resulted in enhanced presynaptic and reduced postsynaptic Wg signaling (Kamimura et al., 2013).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Blocking presynaptic Wg signaling with CA-Sgg did not suppress the loss of boutons or prevent synaptic retraction in trolnull mutants.
source: Blocking presynaptic Wg signaling with CA-Sgg did not suppress the loss of boutons or prevent synaptic retraction in trolnull mutants (Figure 3A–C, p=0.8814 between trol and trol, sggCA bouton numbers).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A–C with statistical comparison provided.

claim: Perlecan's function in controlling synaptic stability is independent of its effects on Wg signaling.
source: These data indicate Perlecan's function in controlling synaptic stability is independent of its effects on Wg signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic interaction experiments showing that blocking Wg signaling does not rescue trol phenotypes.

claim: Control and trolnull larvae had similar NMJ area at the 2nd instar stage when imaging began.
source: Although control and trolnull larvae had similar NMJ area at the 2nd instar stage when imaging began (Figure 4B), only control NMJs continued to grow on subsequent days of imaging (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4B showing no significant difference at 2nd instar.

claim: Only control NMJs continued to grow on subsequent days of imaging after 2nd instar.
source: Although control and trolnull larvae had similar NMJ area at the 2nd instar stage when imaging began (Figure 4B), only control NMJs continued to grow on subsequent days of imaging (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C showing growth in controls but not trol mutants.

claim: Both pre- and postsynaptic area declined in trolnull larvae during the 3rd instar imaging window.
source: In contrast, both pre- and postsynaptic area declined in trolnull larvae during the 3rd instar imaging window.
evidence: The claim is supported by the intravital imaging data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Control NMJs had greater pre- than postsynaptic area, while trolnull larvae had smaller nSybGFP than GluRIIARFP area by the final day of imaging.
source: Control NMJs had greater pre- than postsynaptic area, while trolnull larva had smaller nSybGFP than GluRIIARFP area by the final day of imaging, consistent with loss of presynaptic material and lingering postsynaptic footprints (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Trolnull MNs form NMJs that are subsequently retracted during development.
source: These findings confirm that trolnull MNs form NMJs that are subsequently retracted during development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the serial intravital imaging data showing normal NMJ formation followed by retraction.

claim: At intact trolnull NMJs, nerve stimulation resulted in evoked release amplitude similar to controls.
source: At intact trolnull NMJs, nerve stimulation resulted in evoked release amplitude similar to controls, indicating normal presynaptic output prior to retraction (Figure 4E and F, p=0.3189).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E and F with statistical comparison provided.

claim: Fully retracted trolnull NMJs completely lacked evoked release.
source: In contrast, fully retracted trolnull NMJs completely lacked evoked release (Figure 4E and F, p=0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E and F with statistical comparison provided.

claim: The gradual loss of NMJs is consistent with other cell types where Perlecan is dispensable for the initial formation of BMs and only required for their maintenance.
source: The gradual loss of NMJs is consistent with other cell types where Perlecan is dispensable for the initial formation of BMs and only required for their maintenance (Costell et al., 1999; Matsubayashi et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The largest source of Perlecan in Drosophila comes from the larval fat body, where it is secreted into the hemolymph and incorporated into the ECM surrounding most cell types.
source: The largest source of Perlecan in Drosophila comes from the larval fat body, where it is secreted into the hemolymph and incorporated into the ECM surrounding most cell types (Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Trol mRNA is present at lower levels in larval MNs and muscles.
source: Although abundant in the fat body, trol mRNA is also present at lower levels in larval MNs and muscles (Jetti et al., 2023).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Knockdown of Perlecan with UAS-trol-RNAi.2 driven by multiple cell-type-specific Gal4 lines failed to trigger synaptic retraction or reduce synaptic bouton number.
source: In contrast, knockdown of Perlecan with UAS-trol-RNAi.2 (Figure 1A) driven by multiple Gal4 lines expressed in specific cell populations, including pan-neuronal (elavC155), neuronal and muscle (elavC155 and mef2-Gal4), glial (repo-Gal4), fat body (ppl-Gal4, Lsp2-Gal4), hemocytes (Hml-Gal4), and fat body and hemocytes (c564-Gal4), failed to trigger synaptic retraction or reduce synaptic bouton number (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Knockdown of Perlecan in the three cell types that form or surround NMJs (MNs, muscles and glia) failed to reduce TrolGFP signal around larval nerves or on the muscle surface.
source: In addition, knockdown of Perlecan in the three cell types that form or surround NMJs (MNs, muscles and glia) failed to reduce TrolGFP signal around larval nerves or on the muscle surface (Figure 5C–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C–G.

claim: Perlecan secretion from multiple cell types is required to stabilize NMJs.
source: Together, these data suggest Perlecan secretion from multiple cell types is required to stabilize NMJs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of single cell-type knockdowns to phenocopy the null mutant.

claim: Overexpression of Perlecan specifically in MNs did not rescue the reduction in bouton number or synaptic retraction phenotypes in trolnull larvae.
source: Overexpression of Perlecan specifically in MNs did not rescue the reduction in bouton number or synaptic retraction phenotypes in trolnull larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C, p=0.54 for bouton number with trolRG rescue)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C with statistical comparison provided.

claim: Neuronally secreted Perlecan is insufficient for maintaining synaptic stability.
source: Overexpression of Perlecan specifically in MNs did not rescue the reduction in bouton number or synaptic retraction phenotypes in trolnull larvae (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C, p=0.54 for bouton number with trolRG rescue), suggesting neuronally secreted Perlecan is insufficient for maintaining synaptic stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of neuronal rescue to restore normal phenotype.

claim: Perlecan acts non-cell autonomously from multiple cell types to stabilize larval NMJs.
source: Together, these data indicate Perlecan acts non-cell autonomously from multiple cell types to stabilize larval NMJs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell-type-specific knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Perlecan helps withstand mechanical stress during tissue development in Drosophila and other species.
source: Studies of Perlecan's role within the ECM of other Drosophila cell types and in several mammalian tissues indicate the protein helps withstand mechanical stress during tissue development (Arikawa-Hirasawa et al., 2002; Costell et al., 1999; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Skeath et al., 2017; Töpfer et al., 2022).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: No enhancement of synaptic retraction or decreases in bouton number were observed in trolnull; MhcS1/+ larvae despite increased muscle contraction.
source: Despite increased muscle contraction in trolnull; MhcS1/+ larvae, no enhancement of synaptic retraction or decreases in bouton number were observed (Figure 6A and B, p=0.5975).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6A and B with statistical comparison provided.

claim: No enhancement of Perlecan staining was observed around axons, at NMJs, or on muscles in TrolGFP; MhcS1/+ larvae compared to TrolGFP alone.
source: To examine if muscle hypercontraction increases Perlecan NMJ abundance as a protective mechanism to withstand elevated muscle contraction force, endogenous TrolGFP was brought into the MhcS1 mutant background. No enhancement of Perlecan staining was observed around axons, at NMJs, or on muscles in TrolGFP; MhcS1/+ larvae compared to TrolGFP alone (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 6C–E.

claim: Perlecan is enriched in the neural lamella, a thick ECM structure that surrounds nerve bundles, the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and brain lobes.
source: Within the peripheral nervous system (PNS), Perlecan was enriched in the neural lamella, a thick ECM structure that surrounds nerve bundles, the ventral nerve cord (VNC) and brain lobes (Edwards et al., 1993; Stork et al., 2008).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature describing the neural lamella structure.

claim: Trolnull NMJs within each individual hemisegment displayed similar decreases in synaptic area.
source: Indeed, Trolnull NMJs within each individual hemisegment displayed similar decreases in synaptic area (Figure 7A–C), indicating entire hemisegments undergo coordinated synaptic loss while others remain intact.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A–C.

claim: Entire hemisegments undergo coordinated synaptic loss while others remain intact in trol mutants.
source: Indeed, Trolnull NMJs within each individual hemisegment displayed similar decreases in synaptic area (Figure 7A–C), indicating entire hemisegments undergo coordinated synaptic loss while others remain intact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NMJs within individual hemisegments show similar phenotypes.

claim: Vkg expression in trolnull nerve bundles was dimmer with gaps in staining around axonal segments, along with abnormal aggregation at specific sites along the nerve.
source: In contrast, Vkg expression in trolnull nerve bundles was dimmer with gaps in staining around axonal segments, along with abnormal aggregation at specific sites along the nerve (Figure 8A, B and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8A, B and E.

claim: Vkg staining in axonal cross sections from trolnull larvae showed a thinner, or in some cases absent, neural lamella surrounding Hrp+ axon bundles.
source: Unlike controls, Vkg staining in axonal cross sections from trolnull larvae showed a thinner, or in some cases absent, neural lamella surrounding Hrp +axon bundles (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Anti-Hrp staining was brighter in trolnull axon bundles, suggesting there may be greater antibody penetration in the absence of a functional neural lamella.
source: Anti-Hrp staining was also brighter in trolnull axon bundles, suggesting there may be greater antibody penetration in the absence of a functional neural lamella (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of increased Hrp staining in trol mutants.

claim: Vkg signal around axons was significantly reduced in trolnull larvae, with the Vkg/Hrp ratio significantly lower in trolnull axons than controls.
source: Vkg signal around axons was significantly reduced in trolnull larvae, with the Vkg/Hrp ratio significantly lower in trolnull axons than controls (Figure 8C and D, p=0.0014 and 0.0004).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8C and D with statistical significance values provided.

claim: This phenotype was independent of whether NMJs had undergone retraction, as nerves for both intact and retracted NMJs displayed a reduced neural lamella.
source: This phenotype was independent of whether NMJs had undergone retraction, as nerves for both intact and retracted NMJs displayed a reduced neural lamella.
evidence: This is an observation from the data indicating that neural lamella defects precede NMJ retraction.

claim: Perlecan may play a role in capturing or retaining Vkg within the neural lamella surrounding larval nerves.
source: As such, Perlecan may play a role in capturing or retaining Vkg within the neural lamella surrounding larval nerves.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of abnormal Vkg distribution in trol mutants.

claim: Microtubule bundles in MN axons innervating muscle 4 were examined in larvae expressing vGlut-Gal4; UAS-10xGFP or UAS-myrRFP.
source: Microtubule bundles in MN axons innervating muscle 4 were examined in larvae expressing vGlut-Gal4; UAS-10xGFP or UAS-myrRFP.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: Microtubules in heterozygous trolnull/+ control larvae formed filamentous tracks within axons that extended into synaptic boutons.
source: Microtubules in heterozygous trolnull/+ control larvae formed filamentous tracks within axons that extended into synaptic boutons (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Trolnull axons contained fragmented and non-continuous microtubule tracks or lacked Futsch staining altogether at branch points where the axon exited towards the muscle.
source: In contrast, trolnull axons contained fragmented and non-continuous microtubule tracks or lacked Futsch staining altogether at branch points where the axon exited towards the muscle (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Quantification of Futsch staining intensity in trolnull axons revealed a significant reduction.
source: Quantification of Futsch staining intensity in trolnull axons revealed a significant reduction (Figure 9B, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9B with statistical significance provided.

claim: NMJs undergoing retraction lacked Futsch staining or displayed fragmented microtubules.
source: Similar defects were observed within synaptic terminals, where NMJs undergoing retraction lacked Futsch staining or displayed fragmented microtubules (Figure 9A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Disruptions to the microtubule cytoskeleton within trolnull axons and NMJs accompany synaptic retraction.
source: These data indicate disruptions to the microtubule cytoskeleton within trolnull axons and NMJs accompany synaptic retraction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of microtubule defects in retracting NMJs.

claim: 2nd instar trolnull larvae had some axonal swellings, small RFP+ protrusions beyond the normal nerve boundary, and slightly twisted and disorganized Futsch+ microtubule tracts.
source: 2nd instar trolnull larvae had some axonal swellings, small RFP + protrusions beyond the normal nerve boundary, and slightly twisted and disorganized Futsch + microtubule tracts (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: By early 3rd instar, nerve bundles were disorganized, with numerous protrusions and tangled microtubules.
source: By early 3rd instar, nerve bundles were disorganized, with numerous protrusions and tangled microtubules (Figure 9C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: At the mature 3rd instar stage, some axon bundles were entirely severed, with large tangled nets of disorganized Futsch at the ends of severed nerves.
source: At the mature 3rd instar stage, some axon bundles were entirely severed, with large tangled nets of disorganized Futsch at the ends of severed nerves (Figure 9C–D)
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9C–D.

claim: When nerve bundles in a hemisegment were severed, NMJs in that hemisegment displayed severe retraction.
source: When nerve bundles in a hemisegment were severed, NMJs in that hemisegment displayed severe retraction.
evidence: This is an observation from the data linking axon bundle severing to NMJ retraction.

claim: Single motoneuron labeling with a MN1-Ib Gal4 driver expressing UAS-CD4-TdT to label axons in trolnull larvae revealed discontinuous axon membrane labeling.
source: Single motoneuron labeling with a MN1-Ib Gal4 driver (Aponte-Santiago et al., 2020) expressing UAS-CD4-TdT to label axons in trolnull larvae revealed discontinuous axon membrane labeling (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: The time course of these deficits suggests that axonal damage and breakage occurs upstream of synapse loss.
source: The time course of these deficits suggests that axonal damage and breakage occurs upstream of synapse loss, given that 2nd instar trolnull larvae have normal synaptic area but display altered axonal structure (Figure 9C–D, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal progression of phenotypes observed.

claim: Loss of distal axons following damage is a well-known trigger for neurodegeneration in both invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Loss of distal axons following damage is a well-known trigger for neurodegeneration in both invertebrates and vertebrates (Gerdts et al., 2016; Perlson et al., 2010).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Neurite loss, synaptic retraction and eventual neuronal death following axonal damage often proceeds through a defined molecular cascade known as Wallerian degeneration.
source: Neurite loss, synaptic retraction and eventual neuronal death following axonal damage often proceeds through a defined molecular cascade known as Wallerian degeneration (Coleman and Höke, 2020; Conforti et al., 2014; Llobet Rosell and Neukomm, 2019; Luo and O'Leary, 2005; Sambashivan and Freeman, 2021; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Inhibiting the Wallerian degeneration protein cascade promotes distal axon survival following injury in multiple systems.
source: Inhibiting this protein cascade promotes distal axon survival following injury in multiple systems (DiAntonio, 2019; Fang et al., 2012; Figley et al., 2021; Gerdts et al., 2015; Gilley et al., 2017; Gilley et al., 2015; Llobet Rosell et al., 2022; Neukomm et al., 2017; Sasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Inhibition of the Wallerian degeneration pathway did not rescue distal axon maintenance in trolnull mutants.
source: Inhibition of this pathway did not rescue distal axon maintenance, as trolnull larvae expressing dSarm RNAi still had reduced synaptic bouton number (P=0.5387 between trol and Wallerian degeneration inhibition conditions), with >80% of NMJs displaying postsynaptic footprints associated with synaptic retraction (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9F–H with statistical comparison provided.

claim: Drosophila MNs undergo axonal degeneration and synaptic retraction in trolnull mutants independent of the Wallerian degeneration pathway.
source: These data indicate Drosophila MNs undergo axonal degeneration and synaptic retraction in trolnull mutants independent of the Wallerian degeneration pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of dSarm RNAi to rescue trol phenotypes.

claim: Loss of Perlecan disrupts the neural lamella, leading to axonal damage that causes cytoskeletal disruption and synaptic retraction in a temporally coordinated manner across individual hemisegment nerve bundles during larval development.
source: Together, we conclude that loss of Perlecan disrupts the neural lamella, leading to axonal damage that causes cytoskeletal disruption and synaptic retraction in a temporally coordinated manner across individual hemisegment nerve bundles during larval development (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: In vertebrates, Perlecan loss causes degeneration of the developing heart only after pumping begins.
source: In vertebrates, Perlecan loss causes degeneration of the developing heart only after pumping begins (Costell et al., 1999).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The C. elegans Perlecan homolog Unc-52 regulates a late stage of muscle-epidermis attachment.
source: The C. elegans Perlecan homolog Unc-52 regulates a late stage of muscle-epidermis attachment (Rogalski et al., 2001; Rogalski et al., 1995)
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Within developing Drosophila egg chambers, Perlecan and type IV Collagen function to establish mechanical properties of the ECM, protecting the egg from osmotic stress.
source: Within developing Drosophila egg chambers, Perlecan and type IV Collagen function to establish mechanical properties of the ECM, protecting the egg from osmotic stress (Töpfer et al., 2022).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Within the neural lamella surrounding the Drosophila VNC and brain, Perlecan acts to reduce ECM stiffness established by Vkg and β-integrin.
source: Within the neural lamella surrounding the Drosophila VNC and brain, Perlecan acts to reduce ECM stiffness established by Vkg and β-integrin (Skeath et al., 2017).
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: EM imaging of the VNC neural lamella in trol mutants demonstrates a much thinner ECM.
source: EM imaging of the VNC neural lamella in trol mutants demonstrates a much thinner ECM (Skeath et al., 2017)
evidence: The statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Studies in Drosophila embryos indicate Perlecan is a late delivered component of BMs and ECMs, requiring type IV Collagen for its incorporation into the matrix.
source: Studies in Drosophila embryos indicate Perlecan is a late delivered component of BMs and ECMs, requiring type IV Collagen for its incorporation into the matrix (Matsubayashi et al., 2017; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011).
evidence: The statement is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Perlecan can be produced in numerous cell types in Drosophila, with specific roles requiring secretion from neurons, muscles, glia, hemocytes and fat body, intestinal stem cells, and wing imaginal discs.
source: Perlecan can be produced in numerous cell types in Drosophila, with specific roles requiring secretion from neurons (Cho et al., 2012), muscles (Kamimura et al., 2013), glia (Skeath et al., 2017), hemocytes and fat body (Isabella and Horne-Badovinac, 2015; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Ramos-Lewis et al., 2018), intestinal stem cells (You et al., 2014) and wing imaginal discs (Bonche et al., 2021).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The neural lamella's role in regulating MN axonal and synaptic stability requires Perlecan to act in a non-cell autonomous role and be secreted from multiple cell types.
source: In contrast to these cases of a single cell type supplying the source of Perlecan, the neural lamella's role in regulating MN axonal and synaptic stability requires Perlecan to act in a non-cell autonomous role and be secreted from multiple cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell-type-specific knockdown and rescue experiments.

claim: Multiple cell types are required to secrete Perlecan for proper incorporation and function within the neural lamella.
source: Our data suggest multiple cell types are required to secrete Perlecan for proper incorporation and function within the neural lamella, consistent with examples where multiple cell types are required to secrete Perlecan for its functional role in several contexts (Bonche et al., 2022; Bonche et al., 2021; You et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: Perlecan can act to resist mechanical stress during tissue development in Drosophila and other species by providing malleability to the ECM and BM.
source: Indeed, Perlecan can act to resist mechanical stress during tissue development in Drosophila and other species by providing malleability to the ECM and BM (Costell et al., 1999; Farach-Carson et al., 2014; Khalilgharibi and Mao, 2021; Pastor-Pareja and Xu, 2011; Qin et al., 2014; Ramos-Lewis et al., 2018; Skeath et al., 2017; Töpfer et al., 2022).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Increasing the mechanical stress of muscle contraction with a hyperactive Mhc mutant did not enhance synaptic retraction in trol mutants.
source: However, increasing the mechanical stress of muscle contraction with a previously generated hyperactive Mhc mutant in the lab (Montana and Littleton, 2004) did not enhance synaptic retraction in trol mutants.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing no enhancement of retraction with MhcS1.

claim: The low levels of Perlecan at the NMJ do not appear to be the site of action for how it normally prevents synaptic retraction.
source: Together with the lack of Perlecan enrichment at synaptic boutons, we focused on the neural lamella surrounding nerve bundles as a potential site of action in regulating synaptic stability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of Perlecan enrichment at boutons and the failure of mechanical stress experiments to enhance phenotypes.

claim: MN axons are under constant tension during larval crawling with fixed points of attachment at somas within the VNC and terminal anchors at the NMJ.
source: MN axons are under constant tension during larval crawling with fixed points of attachment at somas within the VNC and terminal anchors at the NMJ (Fan et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2017; Siechen et al., 2009; Tofangchi et al., 2016).
evidence: The statement is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Larval axons degenerated over development in trol mutants.
source: Indeed, larval axons degenerated over development in trol mutants.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations of axonal degeneration.

claim: Imaging of the type IV collagen Vkg revealed reduced Vkg thickness and abnormal accumulation of the protein around nerve bundles in trol mutants.
